newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Finland steps towards Europe's monetary union.
newsitem.headline: Finland steps towards Europe's monetary union.

text.p: Finland demonstrated its determination to join a single European currency at its planned launch in 1999 by agreeing to take the markka into the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM).

The EU's monetary committee decided after nearly five hours of talks in Brussels on Saturday to bring the markka, which had floated for the past four years, into the currency grid at a central rate of 3.04 to the German mark.
The decision, which takes effect on Monday, was hailed as a boost for the prospects of a single European currency and for increased monetary stability on the continent.
By entering the ERM, Finland's coalition government said it wanted to "quarantee that Finland will fulfil all the convergence criteria" for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Currency stability is an EMU criterion and several countries argue that the EU's Maastricht treaty requires ERM membership in order to qualify for the single currency.
The ERM, which limits fluctuations between participating currencies, will now group 11 of the EU's 15 currencies. Italy, Britain, Sweden and Greece remain outside.

The spotlight now turns to the Italian lira, which was forced out of the grid after a currency crisis in 1992. Italy is keen to bring the lira back to bolster its chances of joining a single currency.
The decision by Finland, a relatively new member of the EU, was warmly welcomed by European leaders.
European Commission President Jacques Santer and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said it would help moves towards monetary union.
"The enlargement of the mechanism to include a new currency is a very positive signal on the way to the realisation of the euro (the single currency)," they said in a statement.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said it was an important step for Finland "en route to the European monetary union."

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said it was a positive sign ahead of the creation of the single currency. "The entry shows first and foremost the confidence which exists in the good prospects ahead of the Finnish economy," he said.

The decision underlined the strong recovery and increased stability of the Finnish economy, which suffered a deep crisis in the early 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union, an important export market.
Finland now seems well placed to meet the other EMU criteria on government debt and borrowing, inflation and interest rates.
London-based analysts said the central rate of 3.04 against the mark was a sensible level, even though the markka was trading stronger at 2.986 on Friday.
"Everyone was assuming the markka was going to join soon with a central rate of around 3.03 so this is not a huge surprise," said Stephen King, an economist at HSBC Markets.
The markka will be allowed to fluctuate by up to 15 percent against the other ERM currencies, the normal margins since the bands were widened in August 1993 to deter currency speculation.

The Bank of Finland said it would aim to keep the markka more stable than that. "It will certainly be our policy to keep it within a relatively narrow range," Bank of Finland director Matti Vanhala told Reuters.
In Stockholm, the Swedish central bank said Finland's ERM membership would not affect Sweden's position that it did not have to join the grid to qualify for the new single currency.

The two Nordic nations, which both joined the EU in January last year, are major trading partners as well as fierce competitors on world markets in pulp and paper. Their currencies had floating since Europe's currency turmoil in late 1992.
